title: Sample spaces, events, and probability measures
terms: sample space; outcome; event; algebra of sets; Boolean algebra of sets; sigma-algebra; probability measure; probability space; countable additivity.

exposition.text:
A probability space is (Ω, F, P ), with outcomes ω ∈ Ω, an event sigma-algebra F, and a prob-
ability measure. A sigma-algebra contains Ω and is closed under complements and countable
unions. A Boolean algebra of sets requires only finite unions. The standard measure axioms are
nonnegativity, P(Ω) = 1, and countable additivity on disjoint events.
The book states a finite-additivity version; for general infinite spaces the standard countable
c
form is needed. It yields P (∅) = 0, P(A ) = 1 − P (A), monotonicity, and continuity under
increasing unions or decreasing intersections. A probability-zero event need not be empty, and a
probability-one event need not contain every outcome.
A finite event algebra can be described by its atoms: nonempty events having no smaller
nonempty event in the algebra. Every event is a union of these disjoint atoms. In an infinite
space, closure under finite operations does not imply closure under countable unions. Countable

question.text:
A finite sample space is partitioned into four nonempty blocks. How many events belong to the
sigma-algebra consisting of all unions of these blocks?
(A) 4 (B) 8 (C) 12 (D) 16 (E) 24

solution.text:
Each event is determined uniquely by deciding which of the four disjoint nonempty blocks
4
to include. There are 2 = 16 choices, including the empty union and the whole sample
space.

question.text:
On N, let A consist of finite sets and sets with finite complement. Assign P(A) = 0 to finite
sets and P (A) = 1 to sets with finite complement. Which statement is correct?
(A) A is a sigma-algebra and P is countably additive.
(B) A is an algebra but not a sigma-algebra; P is finitely additive but fails countable additiv-
ity.
(C) A is not closed under complements.
(D) P(N) = 0
(E) P fails finite additivity on disjoint members of A.

solution.text:
Complements and finite unions preserve finite-or-cofinite status. But the union of all even
singletons is neither finite nor cofinite, so the family is not a sigma-algebra. Finite additiv-
ity holds: disjoint cofinite sets cannot both occur, and a finite set disjoint from a cofinite
S
one lies in its finite complement. Countable additivity fails even for the union N = {n},
n
since all singleton values are zero but P(N) = 1.

question.text:
A point is chosen uniformly from [0, 1]. For A = Q ∩ [0, 1] and B = [0, 1] \ Q, which statement is
correct?
(A) P(A) = P(B) = 1/2
(B) P(A) = 0 and A = ∅
(C) P(A) = 0, P(B) = 1, and both events are nonempty
(D) P(A) > 0 because A is infinite
(E) P(B) = 1 implies B = [0, 1]

solution.text:
Each singleton has uniform probability zero. The rational points form a countable union
of such singletons, so countable additivity gives P (A) = 0. Its complement has probability
one. Both sets are nonempty, showing that probability zero does not mean impossible as a
set and probability one does not mean the whole sample space.
